title: The Precious S’s, Part 1: Satisficing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teachers who want to stay sane must practice satisficing, accepting a good-enough option instead of chasing the optimal one, and skipping. Borrowing Herbert Simon's term and Barry Schwartz's research on choice overload, he explains that the trick is knowing when to satisfice and when to do the opposite, maximizing. Satisficing with conviction requires clarity about what your work is for, so he poses questions about your work's purpose and the Everest each lesson climbs toward. Whatever answers those questions earns maximal effort, whether that is content and student knowledge for teachers or leadership study for administrators. He models the discipline by satisficing three or four of his six professional focus areas each year to maximize growth in two or three.
points: Maximize a precious few essential things and satisfice the rest; focus, not triviality, defines a good career.
Schwartz's finding that maximizers suffer most in a culture of abundant choice explains why teachers feel overextended.
You can only satisfice with delight if you are clear about your work's fundamental purpose, so answer the Everest question first.
Even good priorities must be rationed: Stuart intentionally satisfices several of six focus areas each year.
quotes: Satisficing is what we do when we accept an available option as satisfactory rather than working to find or obtain the optimal option. It’s getting gas at the station nearest your house rather than driving all around town to save five cents per gallon.

And the opposite of satisficing is maximizing. We want to maximize the most important, precious, and essential few things, and we want to satisfice or skip the rest. And it’s only by satisficing and skipping the rest that we’re actually able to build lives or careers that are defined by focus versus triviality.

Barry Schwartz argues that “it is maximizers who suffer most in a culture that provides too many choices” (229). Hmm… a culture that provides too many choices… wait, that’s mine! And, if you’re reading this, that’s yours!
The trouble with this counsel is that we can only satisfice with conviction and delight when we’re clear on what it is that we’re about. So answer some questions:

The actions most closely connected to your answers to those questions are the ones you want to maximize. Spend more time understanding your content, understanding students, understanding the art and science of connecting the two. Administrators, spend more time studying leadership, teacher development, and working within crazy constraints.
And you’ve got to be picky. In my book, I recommend six areas for professional focus, and I tend to satisfice 3-4 of those areas each year for the sake of maximizing my growth in 2-3 of them.
